headline: New AI blood test could catch cancer early

sources.title: NHS AI blood test could reduce invasive womb cancer checks
Thousands of women could avoid painful cancer exam with new AI blood test
Thousands of women could be spared painful cancer exam by new NHS AI blood test

chunks.text: Scientists in Britain have {{come up with}} a new blood test that can help find cancer. The test uses artificial intelligence, [[a kind of]] smart computer program, to {{pick up}} [[early signs]] of the [[disease]]. Doctors hope it will {{rule out}} cancer in many patients quickly, so they do not need [[painful]] [[exams]]. It could be good news for women who [[worry about]] [[womb]] cancer.

verbs.correct: To think of a new idea or plan
verbs.why: Come up with means to think of a new plan or solution, often after real effort. Scientists come up with tests, and teams come up with fresh ideas.

verbs.wrong: To take a blood sample from a patient
verbs.why: Here pick up means to notice or detect something small, the way this test picks up early signs of cancer in a blood sample.

verbs.correct: To decide something is not the cause
verbs.wrong: To place a patient in a higher risk group
verbs.why: When doctors rule out cancer, they decide it is not the cause of the symptoms and can stop worrying about it. This new test helps them do that fast.

chunks.text: The test works [[in a simple way]]. A [[nurse]] takes a small [[sample]] of blood from the patient. Then the computer {{looks over}} about 30 [[chemical]] signs in the blood and {{breaks down}} the results into three groups: low [[risk]], medium risk, and high risk. This helps doctors {{narrow down}} which patients [[truly]] need more tests.

verbs.wrong: To print a copy of the results
verbs.why: Look over means to examine something carefully, checking each detail one by one. Here the computer looks over dozens of chemical signs in a blood sample.
Break down means to separate something into smaller parts so it is easier to understand. The computer breaks the results down into three simple risk groups.

verbs.correct: To reduce something to fewer choices
verbs.wrong: To make a test more accurate
verbs.why: Narrow down means to reduce a large group of options to just a few. Doctors use this test to narrow down which patients truly need further exams.

chunks.text: For many patients, this test could {{cut out}} [[the need for]] painful exams. [[Right now]], women with worrying [[symptoms]] often have to {{go through}} an [[uncomfortable]] check at the hospital. The new test is very [[accurate]], and in one large study it [[correctly]] found more than 99 percent of real cancers. It can also {{speed up}} the whole process, so patients do not wait and worry [[for so long]].

verbs.wrong: To perform surgery to remove tissue
verbs.why: Cut out means to remove something completely, so it no longer happens at all. This test could cut out the need for many painful hospital exams.

verbs.wrong: To wait a long time for a result
verbs.why: Go through means to experience something difficult, from a hard illness to an uncomfortable medical exam. Many women go through this kind of check to detect cancer early.

verbs.wrong: To repeat a test more often
verbs.why: Speed up means to make a process happen faster than before. This test can speed up diagnosis, so patients do not wait and worry for weeks.

chunks.text: In a large [[trial]], the test was used on more than 16,000 patients in England, and it costs only about 30 pounds. Some British hospitals have already begun to {{roll out}} the test for their patients. [[Over time]], doctors hope it will {{take on}} other kinds of cancer too, [[such as]] lung and stomach cancer. If it keeps working well, this cheap and simple test may {{catch on}} in hospitals [[around the globe]].

verbs.correct: To introduce something new to people
verbs.wrong: To withdraw a service from hospitals
verbs.why: Roll out means to introduce something new to a group of people, usually gradually. Some British hospitals have already begun to roll out this new blood test.

verbs.wrong: To be replaced by a different test
verbs.why: Take on means to begin to handle a new task or responsibility. Doctors hope this test can take on other cancers too, such as lung and stomach cancer.

verbs.correct: To become popular or widely used
verbs.wrong: To be recalled by the manufacturer
verbs.why: Catch on means to become popular and widely used, often faster than people expect. If it keeps working well, this cheap test may catch on in hospitals everywhere.

mainIdea.s: British scientists made a blood test that uses AI to find early signs of cancer and sort patients by risk. It found over 99 percent of real cancers in a large trial.
mainIdea.why: The article says the test found more than 99 percent of real cancers in a trial of over 16,000 patients. It studies blood samples to sort patients into low, medium, and high risk groups.

mainIdea.s: This new AI blood test already replaces every cancer exam in hospitals nationwide, doctors now say. It already works for every kind of cancer, not just cancer in the womb.
mainIdea.why: Close, but only some hospitals have started using the test, not every hospital nationwide. Doctors also only hope it will work for other cancers like lung and stomach in the future.

mainIdea.s: A separate team of researchers is testing a new vaccine that may help prevent some types of cancer. Early results from that unrelated trial are expected within two years.
mainIdea.why: This is about a different research project on a cancer vaccine, not the AI blood test. The real story is about a blood test that helps doctors avoid painful exams.

tf.s: Scientists came up with a blood test that uses AI to help find cancer.
tf.why: British scientists came up with the new AI blood test to help find cancer early.

tf.s: The test can pick up early signs of cancer from a sample of blood.
tf.why: The test picks up early signs of the disease by studying about 30 chemical signs in the blood.

tf.s: The new test forces every patient to go through more painful exams than before.
tf.why: The test could cut out painful exams, so many patients go through fewer of them, not more.

tf.s: In a large trial, the test correctly found more than 99 percent of real cancers.
tf.why: In a study of more than 16,000 patients, the test found over 99 percent of real cancers.

tf.s: Doctors say the test can only take on womb cancer and no other kind.
tf.why: Doctors hope the test will take on other cancers too, such as lung and stomach cancer.

tf.s: The test is so expensive that hospitals refuse to roll it out.
tf.why: The test costs only about 30 pounds, and some hospitals have already begun to roll it out.
